chunks: What to measure on a motor or solenoid. The question: What properties do you want to measure when using a motor/solenoid?
Before adding sensors to a motor or solenoid, ask what each reading is for.
There are three purposes: protecting it (current, temperature, supply voltage), controlling it (speed, position, torque), and checking its health (power, efficiency, vibration, trends).
Many of these can be worked out from cheap electrical readings. Current is the single most useful one.
Think of a car dashboard. The temperature gauge protects the engine. The speedometer lets you control the car. The trip computer's fuel economy tracks health over time.
The analogy breaks in one useful way: a motor often needs no dedicated gauge, because current and voltage already carry the information.
Three electrical measurements (I, V, R) yield torque, speed, power, heating, stall detection and winding temperature. Dedicated sensors improve accuracy but are not always needed.
Torque constant ( K t ): newton-meters of torque per amp of current. Torque is roughly K t times I . Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates. It tells you speed.
Winding temperature: the hottest, most critical temperature. Copper's resistance rises about 0. 39% per degree Celsius, so resistance reveals it.
Efficiency: mechanical output power divided by electrical input power. Current signature: the shape of coil current over time. A solenoid's shows a dip when the plunger moves.
A motor on 12 volts draws 2 amps while giving 0. 04 N·m at 3000 rpm. Electrical power in is 12 times 2 equals 24 watts.
At 3000 rpm the shaft turns at about 314 rad/s (radians per second; one turn is 2π radians), so power out is 0. 04 times 314 equals 12. 6 watts.
Efficiency is about 52%, and the other 11. 4 watts is heat. Separately, a winding that reads 2. 0 ohms cold and 2. 6 ohms hot has warmed by about 76 degrees Celsius.
That is the whole idea: a few electrical readings give torque, power, and temperature.
"I'd measure by purpose. Protection: current, winding temperature and supply voltage.
Control: speed and position from an encoder or back-EMF, and torque, which comes from current since torque is about Kt times current.
Health: input power, efficiency, vibration, and trends like winding resistance, which also gives temperature.
For solenoids I'd add the current waveform and stroke time to know whether the plunger actually seated. Current is the single most valuable measurement."
Quick check. Which single measurement gives torque, stall detection and overload protection for a DC motor?
